title: Musculoskeletal Neoplasms
subject: Musculoskeletal System (MUSC)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers tumors of bone, cartilage, and soft tissue: the benign bone-forming and cartilage-forming lesions, the primary sarcomas (osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, leiomyosarcoma), the giant cell tumors, metastatic disease in bone, and hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy. Board questions on these tumors almost always supply the same five clues: the patient's age, the bone and the region within it, the x-ray pattern, the matrix or cell the tumor makes, and the gene or marker that confirms it. The chapter explains why each clue points where it does, so you can reason from growth plate biology, bone remodeling, and driver mutations instead of memorizing a list.
prerequisites: Regions of a long bone (epiphysis, physis, metaphysis, diaphysis) and endochondral ossification
Bone remodeling: osteoblasts, osteoclasts, RANKL, osteoprotegerin, and PTH
Tumor suppressor genes, oncogenes, chromosomal translocations, and the two-hit hypothesis
Hematogenous versus lymphatic spread of malignant tumors
Calcium homeostasis: PTH, PTH-related protein (PTHrP), and vitamin D

connections.how: Paget disease drives intense bone turnover and is the main soil for osteosarcoma in older adults.
Ewing sarcoma shares fever, a high ESR, and periosteal reaction with osteomyelitis, so biopsy separates them.
Multiple myeloma is the most common primary malignancy in bone but arises from plasma cells and makes purely lytic lesions.
Prostate carcinoma is the classic osteoblastic metastasis, and the uterus is a main site of leiomyosarcoma.

connections.to: Neoplasms of the pulmonary system and upper respiratory tract (PU-14-F)
connections.how: Lung cancer causes lytic metastases and hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy, and the lung is the usual metastatic target of sarcomas.

terms.def: A malignant tumor of mesenchymal origin, such as bone, cartilage, muscle, fat, fibrous tissue, or vessels.
Unmineralized bone matrix, mainly type I collagen, made by osteoblasts; osteoid made by malignant cells defines osteosarcoma.
The small central focus of osteoid and woven bone in osteoid osteoma, surrounded by reactive sclerotic bone.

A wedge of reactive bone at the edge of a lesion where lifted periosteum meets the cortex, a sign of aggressive growth.
A tumor of small primitive cells with scant cytoplasm and dark nuclei on H and E stain, such as Ewing sarcoma, neuroblastoma, lymphoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma.
A metabolite that accumulates because of a mutant enzyme and promotes tumor growth, such as 2-hydroxyglutarate from mutant IDH1 or IDH2.
A malignant cell showing skeletal muscle differentiation, with eccentric eosinophilic cytoplasm and sometimes cross-striations.

blocks.text: Chondrosarcoma is a malignant tumor whose cells make cartilage matrix but no osteoid. The distinction matters because osteosarcoma may also contain malignant cartilage; if the tumor cells make any osteoid directly, the tumor is classified as osteosarcoma. Chondrosarcoma is the second most common matrix-producing primary malignant bone tumor, about half as frequent as osteosarcoma, and it affects adults, usually in their 40s or older, men more often than women.

It favors the trunk and the proximal limbs: pelvis, shoulder girdle (proximal humerus and scapula), proximal femur, and ribs. This is nearly the reverse of enchondroma, which favors the small bones of the hands and feet, so a cartilage tumor in the pelvis of an adult is regarded as malignant until proven otherwise.
Primary and secondary tumors

Most chondrosarcomas are conventional (hyaline) tumors in the medullary cavity. Primary tumors arise de novo, while secondary tumors arise in a preexisting enchondroma or in the cartilage cap of an osteochondroma (C07). Transformation is rare in a solitary benign lesion and much more likely when there are many lesions, as in Ollier disease, Maffucci syndrome, and hereditary multiple osteochondromas, because every lesion is another chance for further genetic damage. Signs of transformation are new pain in a previously silent lesion, growth after skeletal maturity, cortical destruction, and a soft tissue mass.
IDH mutations

About half of conventional central chondrosarcomas, and most enchondromas, carry a mutation in IDH1 (cytosolic) or IDH2 (mitochondrial). The normal enzyme converts isocitrate to alpha-ketoglutarate. The mutant enzyme gains a new activity and reduces alpha-ketoglutarate to D-2-hydroxyglutarate, which inhibits alpha-ketoglutarate-dependent enzymes such as the TET DNA demethylases and histone demethylases. DNA and histones become hypermethylated, and chondrocytes stay immature and proliferative. Because benign enchondromas carry the same mutation, it is an early event; malignant progression needs more changes, such as loss of CDKN2A. The same oncometabolite operates in some gliomas and in acute myeloid leukemia.

blocks.text: On x-ray, chondrosarcoma is a lytic lesion with ring-and-arc calcification of cartilage lobules, deep scalloping of the inner cortex, and cortical thickening or destruction. Behavior follows histologic grade: low-grade tumors grow slowly and rarely metastasize, while high-grade and dedifferentiated tumors spread through the blood, mainly to the lungs.

Ewing sarcoma is a malignant tumor of primitive small round cells that arises mostly in bone and less often in soft tissue. It is the second most common bone sarcoma of childhood after osteosarcoma. Most patients are 10 to 20 years old, boys slightly more often than girls, and it is much more common in people of European ancestry than of African ancestry. It arises in the diaphysis of long bones, especially the femur, and in the flat bones of the pelvis.
Molecular driver

About 85% of tumors carry t(11;22)(q24;q12), which fuses EWSR1 on chromosome 22 to FLI1 on chromosome 11; most of the rest fuse EWSR1 to ERG, another ETS family gene, on chromosome 21. The chimeric protein joins the EWSR1 activation domain to the FLI1 DNA-binding domain. It binds GGAA repeat sequences, switches on genes that drive proliferation, and represses genes of differentiation. The cell of origin is uncertain, probably a primitive mesenchymal cell. Finding the fusion by FISH or RT-PCR confirms the diagnosis.

blocks.title: From translocation to tumor in Ewing sarcoma
steps: t(11;22) joins EWSR1 to FLI1
Chimeric EWSR1-FLI1 transcription factor forms
Fusion protein binds GGAA repeats across the genome
Growth genes activated, differentiation genes repressed
Primitive small round cells proliferate in marrow
blocks.caption: A translocation creates an aberrant transcription factor that locks primitive cells in a proliferative state.

blocks.text: Microscopically the tumor is sheets of uniform small round cells with scant clear cytoplasm rich in glycogen (PAS positive), sometimes forming Homer Wright rosettes. The cells show strong membranous CD99, which is sensitive but not specific, since lymphoblastic lymphoma and other small round cell tumors can also express it. The differential diagnosis includes neuroblastoma, lymphoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, and small cell osteosarcoma.

The tumor permeates the marrow quickly, producing moth-eaten lytic destruction and a large soft tissue mass. It lifts the periosteum in successive waves, and each wave lays down a thin shell of reactive bone, giving a layered onion-skin periosteal reaction. Patients have pain and swelling, often with fever, anemia, leukocytosis, and a high ESR, because tumor necrosis and cytokines such as IL-6 produce a systemic inflammatory response. This picture closely mimics osteomyelitis, which also causes periosteal reaction. Ewing sarcoma spreads through the blood to the lungs, other bones, and bone marrow.

blocks.predict: A 12-year-old has thigh pain, fever, a high ESR, and a lytic lesion in the femoral shaft with layered periosteal new bone. Two weeks of antibiotics do not help. What would the biopsy most likely show?
blocks.explain: Sheets of small round blue cells with membranous CD99 and an EWSR1-FLI1 fusion. Ewing sarcoma causes fever and inflammatory markers through tumor necrosis and cytokines, and its diaphyseal site and onion-skin reaction fit; osteomyelitis would show neutrophils, necrotic bone, and organisms.
blocks.check: The presentation paragraph and the location of Ewing sarcoma.

blocks.text: Osteoid osteoma is a benign bone-forming tumor less than 2 cm across. It affects teenagers and young adults, males about twice as often as females, and usually arises in the cortex of long bones of the lower limb, especially the femur and tibia. The lesion is a nidus of interlacing trabeculae of woven bone and osteoid lined by plump osteoblasts in a loose, vascular stroma. The surrounding host bone responds by laying down dense reactive bone, which can be much thicker than the nidus itself. On x-ray or CT, a small round lucent nidus, sometimes with a mineralized center, sits inside a zone of cortical sclerosis.
Why the pain responds to NSAIDs

The osteoblasts of the nidus produce large amounts of prostaglandin E2 through cyclooxygenase (COX), and the nidus contains nerve fibers. Prostaglandin E2 sensitizes nociceptors and causes local vasodilation and edema. The result is severe, well-localized pain that is classically worse at night and relieved by aspirin or other NSAIDs, which inhibit COX and remove the source of the prostaglandin.

When osteoid osteoma arises in the posterior elements of a vertebra, it can cause painful scoliosis. Reflex spasm of the paraspinal muscles on the side of the lesion pulls the spine into a curve that is concave toward the lesion.

Osteoblastoma has nearly the same histology, so size and site separate the two. It is larger than 2 cm, favors the posterior elements of the vertebrae (lamina and pedicle), causes a dull aching pain that does not respond to NSAIDs, provokes less reactive sclerosis, and can enlarge and behave in a locally aggressive way.

blocks.title: Osteoid osteoma versus osteoblastoma
rows: Relieved, because the nidus makes prostaglandin E2
Can enlarge and be locally aggressive
blocks.caption: Shared histology (woven bone, osteoid, and osteoblasts in vascular stroma); size, site, and NSAID response distinguish them.

blocks.text: Osteosarcoma is a malignant mesenchymal tumor in which the neoplastic cells make osteoid. It is the most common primary malignant tumor of bone once multiple myeloma is set aside; myeloma is more common, but it is a plasma cell neoplasm that happens to live in marrow rather than a tumor of bone-forming cells. Osteosarcoma has a bimodal age distribution. About 75% of patients are younger than 20 years, and a second peak occurs in older adults, who usually have a predisposing condition such as Paget disease of bone or prior radiation. Males are affected somewhat more often.
Why the knee metaphysis

Most osteosarcomas arise in the metaphysis of long bones, about 60% around the knee (distal femur and proximal tibia), followed by the proximal humerus. These growth plates contribute the most to limb length, so their metaphyses hold the largest population of dividing osteoblastic cells during the adolescent growth spurt, and each division is a chance for a mutation to be copied. The same logic explains the older peak: Paget disease drives intense, disorganized remodeling with high osteoblast turnover, and radiation damages the DNA of cells that keep dividing. In older adults the tumor arises in the pagetic or irradiated bone itself, which is often axial or flat bone.
Pathology and presentation

Grossly the tumor is bulky, gritty, and gray-white with hemorrhage and necrosis. It destroys the cortex and extends into soft tissue; the growth plate and articular cartilage are only relative barriers, so joint invasion is less common. Microscopically, pleomorphic cells with hyperchromatic nuclei, bizarre giant cells, and atypical mitoses make lace-like malignant osteoid. Some tumors also make cartilage or fibrous tissue, but osteoid made directly by the tumor cells defines the diagnosis. Conventional osteosarcoma is intramedullary and high grade. Patients present with a painful, enlarging mass and sometimes a pathologic fracture, and serum alkaline phosphatase is often raised, reflecting osteoblastic activity.

blocks.caption: Both peaks arise where osteoblastic cells divide most, whether from normal growth or from disease.

blocks.text: On x-ray, osteosarcoma is a large destructive lesion with mixed lytic and sclerotic areas, poorly defined margins, cortical breakthrough, and a soft tissue mass. Two periosteal signs are tested. A Codman triangle forms where the tumor has broken through the cortex and lifted the periosteum: at the edge, where the periosteum still meets the cortex at an angle, it lays down a wedge of reactive bone, while centrally the tumor grows too fast for new bone to form. It marks an aggressive process, not osteosarcoma specifically, since Ewing sarcoma, metastases, and osteomyelitis can produce it. A sunburst pattern is made of spicules of mineralized tumor osteoid and reactive bone radiating perpendicular to the cortex into the soft tissue mass. Because the soft tissue component itself mineralizes, the sunburst points strongly toward a bone-forming malignancy.

blocks.title: Periosteal reactions and what they mean
rows: Slow; periosteum has time to make mature bone
Aggressive, with mineralizing tumor in soft tissue
blocks.caption: The slower a lesion grows, the more organized the periosteal bone; aggressive patterns indicate growth rate, not a single diagnosis.

blocks.text: RB1 and TP53

The RB protein, when hypophosphorylated, binds E2F transcription factors and holds the cell in G1. The p53 protein senses DNA damage and halts the cycle through p21 or triggers apoptosis. Losing RB removes the G1 checkpoint, and losing p53 lets damaged cells keep dividing and accumulate chromosomal chaos, a hallmark of osteosarcoma. Germline RB1 mutation (hereditary retinoblastoma) raises osteosarcoma risk many times over, especially within radiation fields, and germline TP53 mutation (Li-Fraumeni syndrome) also predisposes. Sporadic tumors show the same pathways disrupted somatically: RB1 loss, TP53 mutation or MDM2 amplification, and CDKN2A deletion.

blocks.title: Hereditary retinoblastoma and osteosarcoma
steps: Germline RB1 mutation inactivates one allele in every cell
Second hit in a retinal cell causes childhood retinoblastoma
Second hit in a dividing osteoblastic cell removes the G1 checkpoint
Cells enter S phase without control and gather mutations
Osteosarcoma, often in adolescence or a radiation field
blocks.caption: The two-hit model: every cell starts with one hit, so a single somatic event in a dividing bone cell is enough.

blocks.text: Metastasis to lung

Like most sarcomas, osteosarcoma invades thin-walled vessels early and spreads through the blood rather than the lymphatics. Venous blood from the limbs returns to the right heart, so the pulmonary capillaries are the first bed that tumor emboli reach. The lungs are therefore the most common metastatic site, and many patients have microscopic lung metastases at diagnosis; other bones are next.

blocks.title: Reasoning through a bone tumor film
blocks.text: A 16-year-old boy has 2 months of knee pain. X-ray shows a destructive lesion of the distal femoral metaphysis with a Codman triangle and radiating spicules in a soft tissue mass. Step 1, age: a teenager points to osteosarcoma or Ewing sarcoma. Step 2, site: metaphysis favors osteosarcoma, while Ewing sarcoma favors the diaphysis. Step 3, imaging: a Codman triangle says aggressive; a sunburst says the soft tissue mass is mineralizing, which means bone matrix. Step 4, confirmation: biopsy should show pleomorphic cells making osteoid. Step 5, prediction: hematogenous spread makes the lung the first metastatic site. Ask too about family history of retinoblastoma, which would suggest germline RB1.

Rhabdomyosarcoma is a malignant tumor of cells showing skeletal muscle differentiation, and it is the most common soft tissue sarcoma of children and adolescents. It often arises where there is little or no skeletal muscle, such as the bladder and vagina, which suggests it comes from primitive mesenchymal cells that switch on the muscle program rather than from mature muscle. The tumor cell is the rhabdomyoblast, with eccentric eosinophilic cytoplasm containing thick and thin filaments; elongated strap cells and occasional cross-striations may be seen.

blocks.caption: Age, site, and fusion status separate the subtypes; the fusion-positive alveolar type behaves most aggressively in children.

blocks.text: Markers and the alveolar fusion

Desmin is the intermediate filament of all muscle, so it confirms muscle lineage but not which kind. Myogenin (MYF4) and MYOD1 are transcription factors that drive skeletal muscle differentiation, and they appear as nuclear staining, so they identify skeletal muscle specifically. Alveolar tumors typically show strong, diffuse myogenin.

PAX3 and PAX7 are transcription factors of embryonic muscle precursor cells. In the alveolar type, a translocation joins the DNA-binding domain of PAX3 or PAX7 to the potent activation domain of FOXO1. The chimeric protein activates PAX target genes far more strongly than normal, which keeps cells proliferating as precursors that cannot complete differentiation. This explains the aggressive behavior of fusion-positive tumors.

Symptoms follow the site. An orbital tumor causes proptosis, a nasopharyngeal tumor causes nasal obstruction and bleeding, and bladder or vaginal tumors cause hematuria, vaginal bleeding, or a grape-like mass protruding from the vagina. Unlike most sarcomas, rhabdomyosarcoma often reaches regional lymph nodes, especially the alveolar type, in addition to spreading through blood to the lungs.

sections.title: Benign cartilage tumors: osteochondroma and enchondroma

blocks.text: Osteochondroma is the most common benign bone tumor. It is found in adolescents and young adults, males about three times as often as females. It arises from the metaphysis next to the growth plate of long bones, especially around the knee, and grows away from the nearest joint. The lesion is a bony stalk capped by hyaline cartilage, and the cortex and marrow of the stalk are continuous with those of the host bone, which is the key imaging feature. The cap behaves like a growth plate: endochondral ossification at its base builds the stalk, and growth stops when the physes close at skeletal maturity.

About 85% are solitary. Multiple lesions occur in hereditary multiple osteochondromas, an autosomal dominant disorder caused by germline loss-of-function mutations in EXT1 or EXT2; in both settings the cap chondrocytes have lost both copies. EXT1 and EXT2 encode glycosyltransferases that build heparan sulfate chains on proteoglycans. Heparan sulfate shapes the diffusion and signaling of Indian hedgehog in the growth plate, so without it chondrocytes lose their orientation and a clone grows sideways out of the physis. Patients with the hereditary form have many lesions, short stature, and limb deformities.

Enchondroma is a benign nodule of hyaline cartilage inside the medullary cavity, probably derived from growth plate cartilage that was never replaced by bone. It appears from the 20s to the 50s and is most common in the short tubular bones of the hands and feet. It is usually solitary and painless, found incidentally or after a pathologic fracture of a finger. The x-ray shows a well-defined central lucency with ring-and-arc calcification, a thin intact cortex, and no periosteal reaction. Most enchondromas carry IDH1 or IDH2 mutations (C01).

Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome are forms of enchondromatosis, with multiple enchondromas that often favor one side of the body. They are not inherited; they result from a postzygotic, mosaic IDH1 or IDH2 mutation, which explains the patchy distribution. Maffucci syndrome adds soft tissue hemangiomas and a risk of other tumors such as brain gliomas. Both carry a substantial risk of chondrosarcoma because of the number of lesions.

sections.title: Giant cell tumor of bone and tenosynovial giant cell tumor

blocks.text: Giant cell tumor of bone is a benign but locally aggressive tumor of adults aged about 20 to 40 years, slightly more often women. It arises after the growth plate has closed, in the epiphysis, and extends into the metaphysis up to the subchondral bone beneath the joint. About half occur around the knee, and the distal radius and proximal humerus are next. The x-ray shows an eccentric, expansile, purely lytic lesion with a thin shell of reactive bone and no matrix mineralization, the soap-bubble appearance. Because it lies against the joint, it can cause pain that mimics arthritis, and it may present with pathologic fracture.
Who does the damage

The tumor contains two cell populations. The neoplastic cells are mononuclear stromal cells of osteoblast lineage, most of which carry a mutation in the histone gene H3-3A (formerly H3F3A, G34W). They express RANKL, which binds RANK on monocyte-macrophage precursors and drives them to fuse into large, non-neoplastic osteoclast-like giant cells with many nuclei. These giant cells resorb the bone. The mechanism is confirmed by RANKL blockade with an antibody such as denosumab, which makes the giant cells disappear. The tumor often recurs locally and rarely sends slow-growing deposits to the lung.

Tenosynovial giant cell tumor is a benign neoplasm of the synovium of joints, bursae, and tendon sheaths, usually in adults aged about 20 to 50. The localized type is a small, firm nodule on a tendon sheath, most often of the fingers and hand. The diffuse type, formerly called pigmented villonodular synovitis, involves a large joint, most often the knee, as brown villous synovium that causes recurrent bloody effusions and can erode bone.

Most tumors carry a translocation, often t(1;2) joining CSF1 to the COL6A3 promoter, that causes overexpression of colony-stimulating factor 1. Only a minority of cells carry it. The secreted CSF1 recruits macrophages bearing the CSF1 receptor, which make up most of the mass, so the tumor is largely reactive cells gathered by a few neoplastic ones. Repeated bleeding loads these macrophages with hemosiderin, explaining the brown color, foam cells, and multinucleated giant cells.

blocks.title: Two giant cell tumors compared
rows: Mononuclear stromal cell with H3-3A mutation
Soap-bubble lytic lesion to subchondral bone
blocks.caption: In both, a small neoplastic population secretes a signal that recruits the reactive cells forming most of the tumor.

blocks.text: Metastases are the most common malignant tumors in bone, far outnumbering primary bone sarcomas. Two facts explain this. Carcinomas are much more common than sarcomas, which make up only about 1% of adult cancers. And red marrow is fertile soil: it receives high blood flow through slow sinusoids with fenestrated endothelium, and its matrix stores growth factors that tumor cells can use. Metastases therefore settle in bones that keep red marrow in adults, the vertebrae, pelvis, ribs, skull, and proximal femur and humerus, and are uncommon beyond the elbow and knee. The valveless vertebral venous plexus (Batson plexus) connects pelvic and breast veins to the spine, so a rise in abdominal pressure can carry prostate or breast cancer cells straight to the vertebrae. In adults most bone metastases come from prostate, breast, kidney, lung, and thyroid; in children, from neuroblastoma, Wilms tumor, and rhabdomyosarcoma.
Lytic, blastic, and mixed lesions

The pattern depends on which bone cell the tumor drives. Lytic tumors secrete PTHrP and cytokines such as IL-6 and TNF, which raise RANKL on osteoblasts and stromal cells; osteoclasts then resorb bone and release stored TGF-beta and IGF, which stimulate the tumor further. This loop is called the vicious cycle. Prostate cancer instead secretes osteoblast stimulants such as endothelin-1 and bone morphogenetic proteins, so osteoblasts lay down dense woven bone around the deposits.

blocks.title: The vicious cycle of osteolytic metastasis
steps: Tumor cells in marrow secrete PTHrP and cytokines

Osteoclasts form and resorb bone
Matrix releases TGF-beta, IGF, and calcium
Growth factors stimulate tumor growth and more PTHrP
blocks.caption: Bone destruction feeds the tumor, and the tumor drives more bone destruction.

Most common source of bone metastasis in women

blocks.text: Complications and laboratory findings

Lytic lesions remove load-bearing cortical bone, so pathologic fracture is common, especially in the femur and spine, where vertebral collapse can compress the spinal cord. Blastic lesions also fracture, because the new woven bone is poorly organized. Hypercalcemia results from local osteolysis and from tumor PTHrP acting on bone and kidney; in either case PTH is suppressed by negative feedback. Alkaline phosphatase rises with osteoblast activity, so it is high in blastic disease. A technetium-99m phosphonate bone scan shows sites of active new bone formation, so blastic lesions show strongly while purely lytic lesions may be missed. Marrow replacement can cause a leukoerythroblastic blood picture.

blocks.predict: Why might a bone scan miss the lesions of multiple myeloma yet show those of prostate cancer clearly?
blocks.explain: The tracer binds where osteoblasts are mineralizing new bone. Prostate deposits stimulate osteoblasts, while myeloma suppresses them and activates osteoclasts, leaving purely lytic holes with little new bone.
blocks.check: The table of patterns and the laboratory paragraph.

blocks.title: Two patients with bone lesions and different calcium
blocks.text: Patient A, a 70-year-old man, has back pain, sclerotic lumbar vertebrae, high alkaline phosphatase, and normal calcium. Osteoblasts are building bone, consuming calcium and releasing alkaline phosphatase, which fits prostate cancer. Patient B, a 62-year-old smoker, has lytic rib lesions, serum calcium 13.5 mg/dL (reference about 8.5 to 10.5), and low PTH. Osteoclasts are releasing calcium faster than the kidney can excrete it, and tumor PTHrP may add a systemic effect; the high calcium suppresses PTH. The opposite PTH result, high calcium with high PTH, would point to primary hyperparathyroidism instead.

sections.title: Soft tissue sarcomas by lineage, and spread to lung

blocks.text: Soft tissue sarcomas are classified by the normal tissue the tumor cells resemble, not by where they arise. Under the light microscope many sarcomas look alike, as sheets of spindle or round cells, so immunohistochemistry identifies the lineage by the proteins the cells make. Intermediate filaments mark broad families: vimentin is found in mesenchymal cells generally, and desmin in muscle of every type. Contractile proteins and lineage transcription factors then narrow the answer to skeletal or smooth muscle.

blocks.title: Muscle lineage markers
blocks.caption: Desmin says muscle; myogenin says skeletal muscle; smooth muscle actin and h-caldesmon say smooth muscle.

blocks.text: Leiomyosarcoma

Leiomyosarcoma is a malignant tumor of smooth muscle cells that occurs in adults, usually from middle age onward. Common sites are the retroperitoneum, the uterus (where it is the most common sarcoma), the walls of large veins such as the inferior vena cava, and the deep soft tissue of the limbs. The cells form fascicles of spindle cells with eosinophilic fibrillar cytoplasm and blunt-ended, cigar-shaped nuclei. Because benign leiomyomas share this appearance, malignancy is judged by nuclear atypia, high mitotic activity, and coagulative tumor necrosis. Uterine leiomyosarcoma usually arises on its own rather than from a leiomyoma, and it is typically a single soft, hemorrhagic, necrotic mass in a postmenopausal woman, in contrast to the multiple firm, whorled leiomyomas of reproductive age. Its karyotype is complex, and TP53 and RB1 are often lost.
Why sarcomas spread to the lung

Carcinomas arise in epithelium beside a dense lymphatic network and usually reach regional lymph nodes first. Sarcomas arise in mesenchyme, where tumor cells grow around and into thin-walled vessels early, so they spread mainly through the blood. Venous blood from the limbs, retroperitoneum, and uterus returns through the systemic veins to the right heart, making the pulmonary capillaries the first bed tumor emboli meet. The lung is therefore the usual first metastatic site of sarcomas, often as multiple rounded nodules. Exceptions follow the same logic: sarcomas drained by the portal vein, such as those of the bowel wall, seed the liver first, and a few sarcomas, including rhabdomyosarcoma and synovial sarcoma, often reach lymph nodes.

Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy (HPOA) is a syndrome of digital clubbing, periosteal new bone formation along the shafts of tubular bones (radius, ulna, tibia, fibula, and the metacarpals and metatarsals), and a symmetric arthritis or arthralgia of the neighboring joints, such as the wrists, knees, and ankles. The secondary form is a paraneoplastic syndrome, most often of non-small cell lung carcinoma, especially adenocarcinoma, and also of pleural tumors. Non-malignant causes include cyanotic congenital heart disease, cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis, and lung abscess. A rare primary form, pachydermoperiostosis, is inherited through mutations in HPGD or SLCO2A1, genes needed to take up and degrade prostaglandin E2.
Mechanism

The leading explanation centers on platelets and growth factors. Megakaryocytes released from the marrow normally lodge in the pulmonary capillaries, where they fragment into platelets. When they bypass this filter, through right-to-left shunting or abnormal tumor vessels, large megakaryocytes and platelet clumps impact in the small vessels of the fingertips and the periosteum. There they release platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), which promote vessel growth, edema, and fibroblast and osteoblast proliferation. Tumors also secrete VEGF, and prostaglandin E2 rises when the lung fails to clear it, as the primary form demonstrates. The findings often regress after the tumor is removed.

Megakaryocytes and platelet clumps reach systemic circulation

blocks.caption: A widely accepted but not fully proven model linking intrathoracic disease to changes in the distal limbs.

blocks.text: In clubbing, the soft tissue under the nail bed thickens, so the angle between the nail plate and the proximal nail fold rises to more than 180 degrees, the nail bed feels spongy, and the normal diamond-shaped gap between opposed fingernails disappears (Schamroth sign). X-rays show a smooth line of new periosteal bone along the shafts, separated from the cortex by a thin lucent line, usually symmetric. A bone scan shows symmetric linear uptake along the cortices. Joint fluid is usually non-inflammatory. Uncomplicated COPD does not cause clubbing, so new clubbing in a smoker suggests lung cancer.

blocks.title: Paraneoplastic syndromes of lung cancer
rows: Antibodies to presynaptic voltage-gated Ca2+ channels
blocks.caption: HPOA is the musculoskeletal member of this group and, unlike the endocrine syndromes, is most linked to non-small cell tumors.

integration.text: Normal bone biology predicts most bone tumors. Tumors arise where cells divide: osteosarcoma in growing metaphyses and remodeling pagetic bone, osteochondroma and enchondroma from growth plate cartilage that grew sideways or was left behind. Location follows marrow and blood flow, so metastases seek red marrow and Ewing sarcoma permeates the diaphyseal marrow. The RANKL system that normally couples osteoblasts to osteoclasts is hijacked by giant cell tumor of bone and by lytic metastases, and the same signal explains hypercalcemia. Periosteal reactions record growth rate, which is why the same pattern can appear in infection and malignancy.

Molecular pathology confirms the diagnosis and explains behavior. Fusion genes (EWSR1-FLI1, PAX3 or PAX7 to FOXO1, CSF1 rearrangement) create abnormal transcription factors or growth signals; loss of RB1 and TP53 links osteosarcoma to hereditary retinoblastoma and Li-Fraumeni syndrome; and IDH mutations tie cartilage tumors to gliomas and leukemia through a shared oncometabolite. Markers are tools with limits: CD99 and desmin are sensitive but not specific, and imaging signs such as the Codman triangle signal aggressiveness rather than a single diagnosis, so tissue diagnosis remains the final step.

summary: Location narrows bone tumors: epiphysis for giant cell tumor, metaphysis for osteosarcoma and osteochondroma, diaphysis for Ewing sarcoma, medulla of hand bones for enchondroma, cortex for osteoid osteoma.
Osteosarcoma is defined by tumor cells making osteoid, peaks in adolescents at the knee and in older adults with Paget disease or radiation, and is linked to RB1 and TP53 loss.
A Codman triangle signals aggressive periosteal lifting; a sunburst signals mineralizing tumor in soft tissue; onion skin signals growth in repeated waves.
Ewing sarcoma is a CD99-positive small round blue cell tumor driven by EWSR1-FLI1 from t(11;22), and its fever and high ESR mimic osteomyelitis.
Chondrosarcoma affects older adults in the pelvis and shoulder girdle, may arise from enchondroma or osteochondroma, and often carries IDH1 or IDH2 mutations that produce 2-hydroxyglutarate.
Osteoid osteoma is a nidus under 2 cm whose prostaglandin E2 causes night pain relieved by NSAIDs; osteoblastoma is larger, vertebral, and not NSAID-responsive.
Osteochondroma (EXT1 or EXT2) is a stalk with a cartilage cap continuous with host marrow; enchondroma is intramedullary cartilage, multiple in Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome.
In giant cell tumor of bone, RANKL from neoplastic stromal cells recruits the osteoclast-like giant cells; in tenosynovial giant cell tumor, CSF1 recruits macrophages.
Metastases are the most common malignant tumors in bone: prostate is blastic, kidney, thyroid, and lung are lytic, and breast is mixed; lysis causes fracture and hypercalcemia with suppressed PTH.
Desmin marks muscle, myogenin skeletal muscle, and smooth muscle actin smooth muscle; sarcomas spread through blood to the lung, and HPOA is a paraneoplastic sign of lung cancer.

verify: Frequencies are approximate and vary among sources: chondrosarcoma about half as common as osteosarcoma, about 75% of osteosarcomas before age 20 and about 60% around the knee, about 85% of Ewing sarcomas with EWSR1-FLI1, about half of central chondrosarcomas with IDH mutations, and about 85% of osteochondromas solitary.
The size cutoff between osteoid osteoma and osteoblastoma is given as 2 cm in most texts but 1.5 cm in some; confirm the value NABNE uses.

Rates of malignant change in solitary osteochondroma, hereditary multiple osteochondromas, and Ollier disease or Maffucci syndrome differ widely between series, so no percentages are stated here; confirm whether NABNE expects figures.
The megakaryocyte, PDGF, VEGF, and prostaglandin E2 model of hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy is the leading hypothesis, not an established mechanism.
The H3-3A (H3F3A) G34W mutation in giant cell tumor of bone and the CSF1 rearrangement in tenosynovial giant cell tumor reflect current WHO classification; older texts may not include them.

Breast metastases are called mixed in some sources and predominantly lytic in others, and some lung cancers (for example small cell and carcinoid) can produce blastic deposits; confirm the classification NABNE expects.

Terminology has changed: hereditary multiple exostoses is now hereditary multiple osteochondromas, and pigmented villonodular synovitis is now diffuse tenosynovial giant cell tumor; confirm which names NABNE uses.
Prognosis by rhabdomyosarcoma subtype (botryoid best, alveolar worse) follows Robbins; current risk grouping also uses fusion status, stage, and site.
The size of the increased osteosarcoma risk with germline RB1 mutation is quoted from several hundredfold to about 1000-fold in different sources, so no figure is stated here.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: bone-tumor-map (long bone with epiphysis, metaphysis, diaphysis, cortex, and medulla, showing the usual site of each tumor) and periosteal-reactions (solid, lamellated, Codman triangle, and sunburst patterns side by side).
